title: They Never Taught Us How to Lead.
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: O'Brien argues that new principals are not under-prepared but never exposed to the actual work of running a school: hiring systems, feedback cadences, meeting design, developing other leaders. Preparation programs teach policy, law and leadership styles, so principals imitate the visible style of admired leaders while the invisible systems behind that style go unseen. Without architecture, they run everything personally, and the usual outcomes are lost staff trust, burnout or exit. He reframes the principal as Chief Systems Officer, whose three verbs are design the system, monitor the system and coach the people inside it. He sketches six systems (personal, people, instructional, student culture, communication, school improvement) and says the personal system comes first. He draws on his own early years as a heroic, do-everything principal, and previews a series and book on the framework.
points: Principal preparation teaches what leadership looks like (styles, theory, policy) but almost nothing about what it builds, so new principals copy observable style rather than designing systems.
A school that runs on one person's presence is always one bad week from dysfunction, and the predictable results are eroded trust, burnout or quitting.
When something breaks, the Chief Systems Officer asks which system let the ball drop rather than who dropped it, a more demanding question that produces improvement.
The framework reduces the job to three verbs (design, monitor, coach) across six systems, beginning with the principal's own time, energy and boundaries.
Student culture is treated as a set of designed routines installed in the first eighteen days, not a vibe managed reactively.
quotes: Insufficient preparation implies the right content was present but thin. Never exposed means the content didn’t exist in the curriculum at all. The gap isn’t a gap in depth.

You can watch a great principal work a room and see confidence, warmth, precision, presence. You cannot see the hiring rubric they built, the observation schedule they designed, the meeting architecture that keeps six systems running simultaneously without requiring their personal heroism to hold it together.
Style is what leadership looks like. Systems are what leadership produces.
Because heroism is not a sustainable fuel source for a marathon. The principal who is running everything has no system for protecting their own energy, their own time, their own capacity to lead.
Their job is to ensure that six systems are functioning to their full capability — and when they aren’t, to fix the system rather than the individual inside it. That one shift changes everything.
That question is not softer. It is more demanding. And it produces something the blame model never does: a school that actually gets better.
Culture is not a vibe. It is a set of designed routines, responses, and relationships that produce a predictable, safe, affirming environment for every student every day.
